title: E.m.f., potential difference and energy transfer

learning_outcomes.text: define and use the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source as energy transferred per unit charge in driving charge around a complete circuit
distinguish between e.m.f. and potential difference (p.d.) in terms of energy considerations

external_knowledge: Topic 9: electric charge is measured in coulombs.
Topic 9: potential difference is measured in volts and by a voltmeter connected across two points.
Topic 9: current is measured by an ammeter in the current path.

prior_knowledge_summary: Lesson 1 established prescribed circuit symbols, complete loops, branches and junctions.
Lesson 1 established that a voltmeter connects across the two terminals of the component whose potential difference is measured.
Topic 9 supplied charge in coulombs and the measurement roles of ammeters and voltmeters.
new_learning: Interpret e.m.f. as source energy supplied per unit charge around a complete circuit.
Interpret potential difference as energy transferred from electrical energy per unit charge between two points.
Use V = W/Q and the equivalent energy relationships ΔE = VQ and ΔE = 𝓔Q.
Distinguish the energy-gain role of an ideal source from the energy-transfer role of a component.
not_yet_taught: internal resistance and terminal potential difference
variation of terminal potential difference with current
derivations for series or parallel resistance

blocks.heading: Where did each joule go?
content: An ideal 6.0 V battery drives 1.0 C of charge around a complete loop containing two lamps. The battery gives the charge 6.0 J of electrical energy. One lamp receives 2.0 J and the other receives 4.0 J. Why can all three devices have different voltage labels without any energy disappearing?
Predict what a voltage label tells us about energy. The answer is not the amount of charge and not the rate of flow. It compares an energy transfer with the charge involved.

figure.purpose: Create the need to interpret source e.m.f. and component p.d. through energy per unit charge.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of one ideal battery and two lamps in a complete loop. Track a 1.0 C charge packet receiving 6.0 J at the battery, then transferring 2.0 J and 4.0 J at the lamps. Use restrained colour arrows for energy gain and energy transfer. Do not introduce internal resistance or loop equations.
figure.alt_text: A one-coulomb charge packet gains six joules at an ideal battery and transfers two joules and four joules at two lamps.

blocks.heading: E.m.f. describes what the source supplies
content: Inside a cell or battery, another energy store decreases. For a chemical cell, chemical energy is transferred to electrical energy. The source drives charge around the complete circuit.
The controlled definition to remember is: energy transferred by a source from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge driven around a complete circuit.

The definition ID is 9702_def_electromotive_force. E.m.f. is written as 𝓔 and measured in volts. One volt is one joule per coulomb, so a 6.0 V source supplies 6.0 J to each coulomb that it drives around the complete circuit.
Treat every source in this lesson as ideal. We are not yet considering energy transfer inside the source or a changing terminal reading.

controlled_knowledge.displayed_definition: energy transferred by a source from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge driven around a complete circuit

figure.purpose: Show e.m.f. as an energy-gain process at a source rather than a force or a store of charge.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper energy-account sketch. Show a chemical energy store feeding an ideal cell, a 1 C charge packet crossing the source, and an electrical-energy arrow labelled 𝓔 joules per coulomb. Include a small complete-loop outline to support the definition. Avoid internal-resistance symbols.
figure.alt_text: Chemical energy becomes electrical energy as one coulomb passes through an ideal source in a complete circuit.

blocks.heading: Potential difference describes what is transferred between two points
content: When charge passes through a lamp, resistor or motor, electrical energy is transferred to other forms. A lamp transfers energy to light and thermal energy. A motor transfers energy to kinetic and thermal energy.
The controlled definition to remember is: energy transferred per unit charge. The definition ID is 9702_def_potential_difference.
Potential difference belongs between two points. A voltmeter connects across those two points because it compares the electrical energy per unit charge at its two terminals.
For a 3.0 V p.d. across a lamp, each coulomb transfers 3.0 J from electrical energy while moving through the lamp. The charge is not used up. Its electrical energy changes.

figure.purpose: Give a second energy-per-charge picture for p.d. and connect it to Lesson 1 voltmeter endpoints.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper before-and-after charge-packet sketch across a lamp. Mark the two lamp terminals and a voltmeter connected across them. Show a 1 C packet losing 3.0 J of electrical energy while light and thermal arrows leave the lamp. Keep current and resistance calculations absent.
figure.alt_text: A voltmeter spans a lamp as each coulomb transfers three joules to light and thermal energy.

blocks.heading: Use voltage as joules per coulomb
content: The formula to remember for potential difference is V = W/Q. This is controlled formula 9702_formula_potential_difference. V is potential difference in volts, W is energy transferred or work done in joules, and Q is charge in coulombs.
A heater has a p.d. of 9.0 V and 24 C passes through it. Rearranging is not needed here: W = VQ = 9.0 × 24 = 216 J. The heater receives 216 J of electrical energy.
Check the units independently: V × C = (J C⁻¹) × C = J. Also, 24 packets of one coulomb each transfer 9.0 J, so an answer a little above 200 J is sensible.

The equivalent energy formulas to remember are ΔE = VQ and ΔE = 𝓔Q. They form controlled formula 9702_formula_energy_charge_potential_difference. Use V for a transfer across two points and 𝓔 for energy supplied by a source.

figure.purpose: Model a complete energy calculation with symbols, substitution, units and an independent check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated worked layout in four rows: known V and Q, choose ΔE = VQ, substitute 9.0 × 24, then unit and magnitude checks. Use hand-drawn boxes and a small heater icon. Do not use the same numbers as any practice question.
figure.alt_text: A worked layout calculates 216 joules transferred when 24 coulombs cross a nine-volt heater.

blocks.heading: The same charge can gain energy and transfer it
content: Imagine following one coulomb around an ideal source and a buzzer. At the source, the coulomb gains electrical energy supplied from the source's chemical store. At the buzzer, electrical energy is transferred to sound and thermal energy.

This gives the key distinction. E.m.f. describes energy transferred to the electrical pathway by the source per unit charge around the complete circuit. Potential difference describes energy transferred from the electrical pathway per unit charge between selected points.

In a loop with more than one component, the p.d. across one component may be less than the source e.m.f. because some of the supplied energy per coulomb is transferred in the other components. We use only this energy account here, not Kirchhoff equations.

For an ideal source and a single external component, the source may supply 5.0 J per coulomb and that component may transfer the same 5.0 J per coulomb. Equal numerical values do not make e.m.f. and p.d. the same process.

figure.purpose: Contrast the direction and location of source energy supply with component energy transfer.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper split comparison following the same 1 C marker. Left: it gains electrical energy crossing an ideal source. Right: it transfers electrical energy in a buzzer as sound and thermal energy. Use arrows with distinct colours and the labels 'source supplies' and 'component transfers'.
figure.alt_text: The same one-coulomb packet gains electrical energy at a source and transfers it in a buzzer.

blocks.heading: Voltage is not energy and e.m.f. is not a force
content: It feels natural to say a 6.0 V battery contains 6.0 J or gives every charge 6.0 J. That misses the words per unit charge. A 6.0 V battery supplies 6.0 J for each coulomb, so 3.0 C receives 18 J.
The name electromotive force is historical. E.m.f. is measured in volts, not newtons, and its meaning is an energy transfer per unit charge. It is not a mechanical force on a component.

Another tempting idea is that a component uses up charge. Charge continues around a complete circuit. A component receives electrical energy from that charge. Tracking coulombs separately from joules prevents this mistake.

figure.purpose: Repair confusion between volts, joules, coulombs and force units.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper error-correction panel. Cross out '6 V = 6 J' and replace it with '6 V = 6 J C⁻¹'. Show three 1 C packets each receiving 6 J, totalling 18 J, and a small note that e.m.f. has unit V rather than N. Avoid practice-question numbers.
figure.alt_text: A correction panel shows that six volts means six joules per coulomb, not six joules or six newtons.

blocks.heading: Track source, charge and energy
content: First locate the process. If a source transfers other energy into electrical energy and drives charge around the complete circuit, use e.m.f. If a component transfers electrical energy between two points, use potential difference.
Second translate volts into joules per coulomb. Then choose ΔE = 𝓔Q for a source or ΔE = VQ for a component. Keep Q in coulombs and energy in joules.

Third check the story. Source energy should decrease when the source supplies energy. A component should receive the energy form named in the context. The charge itself is conserved rather than consumed.
This lesson treats the source as ideal. The next lesson adds internal resistance and explains why terminal p.d. can differ from e.m.f. when current flows. Do not use that later model yet.

concepts_taught: ideal-source energy supply per unit charge
component energy transfer per unit charge
charge is conserved while electrical energy is transferred
misconceptions_addressed: A voltage value is an amount of energy rather than energy per unit charge.
E.m.f. is a mechanical force measured in newtons.
Charge is used up when a component transfers electrical energy.
Equal numerical values make e.m.f. and p.d. the same physical process.
next_lesson_can_assume: E.m.f. is source energy supplied per unit charge around a complete circuit.
Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge between two points.
ΔE = 𝓔Q and ΔE = VQ can be used with joules and coulombs.
For an ideal source, e.m.f. and component p.d. can be compared through an external energy account.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Internal resistance or energy transfer inside a source.
Variation of terminal p.d. with current.
Kirchhoff's laws or general resistor-network methods.
